transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-02-05 15:30 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes (recording)
Attendees: Jordan Reyes (Redwood AE), Priya Banerjee (Redwood SE), Carlos Mendez (Acadia CTO), Lina Zhou (Platform), Evan Park (SRE)

Summary:
Quick integration/discovery to understand Acadia's requirements for SDK usage, gateway/proxy patterns, rate-limiting and observability hooks. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private deployment options and scoped an initial benchmark POC.

Topics: SDKs (Python/Node), LangChain/LlamaIndex connectors, sidecar vs centralized gateway, rate limits/quotas (token rps, burst), observability (traces, token-level cost), security (SOC2, KMS, VPC).

Transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Reyes: Hey everyone, thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call, then Priya's going to walk through integration patterns we've seen with customers. Uh, hi Carlos, Lina, Evan.
[00:12] Carlos Mendez: Hi Jordan, yeah thanks. We, uh, pulled Lina and Evan in cause they're the ones who will own the infra changes.
[00:18] Priya Banerjee: Cool. Real quick context: Acadia, you mentioned a few things in the form — heavy vector search we assume, LlamaIndex in the retrieval stack?
[00:26] Lina Zhou: Yeah, we're using LlamaIndex (or, the transcribed notes: Lama Index haha), plus a homegrown embedding pipeline. Most calls originate from our API gateway and then fan out.
[00:34] Evan Park: We see a median prompt length around 350 tokens, heavy tails to 2k for long docs. Around 80 rps peak for a single product endpoint.
[00:44] Jordan Reyes: Great, that's helpful. Two immediate questions: 1) do you want Redwood hosted first for speed of integration, or are you already constrained by compliance such that Private / VPC is required? 2) do you plan to run a gateway / proxy at product edge, or route requests directly to Redwood?
[01:02] Carlos Mendez: We're evaluating both. CTO call tends to prefer hosted for velocity but security has pushed for VPC. For initial pilot we want hosted but with an option to move to Dedicated or Private if we see performance or compliance reasons.
[01:18] Priya Banerjee: That's a common approach — start hosted then gradationally migrate. On the SDK side, Redwood has official Python and Node clients, and we maintain connectors for LangChain and LlamaIndex. The Lang Chain connector supports the new function-calling and streaming semantics.
[01:38] Lina Zhou: Does the LangChain connector preserve chunked streaming? We rely on streaming for the UI.
[01:44] Priya Banerjee: Yes, streaming is supported. There are small caveats with continuous batching — if you need strict per-token latency we can tune batch windows or opt for a sticky routing to avoid batching for certain routes.
[01:58] Evan Park: Okay, about gateway patterns: currently we do JWT auth at our edge and then hit the models via a central service. We also do rate limiting at the gateway. Would Redwood's rate limits be redundant?
[02:10] Jordan Reyes: You can do both. Many customers keep edge-level rate limits for business rules and also enforce token-level quotas at Redwood to protect model pools (especially on shared hosted plans). Dedicated pools let you configure higher throughput and different quota semantics.
[02:26] Carlos Mendez: Can you explain quota types? We saw "per-account per-second token" in the docs but want to map to our users and API keys.
[02:34] Priya Banerjee: Sure. We have: per-api-key rate limits, project-wide token budgets, and optional per-user quotas — the latter can be implemented by tagging requests with user_id metadata so billing and quotas line up. For Dedicated you can also disable soft throttles and enable guaranteed burst capacity.
[02:54] Lina Zhou: How do we tag requests? Header?
[02:58] Priya Banerjee: Yes header X-Redwood-User or in the SDK call. We also surface token-level breakdown in the Console and via the /usage API.
[03:10] Evan Park: Observability — we need traces tied back to our spans. Do you integrate with OpenTelemetry?
[03:16] Priya Banerjee: We do. You can send OTLP traces to your tracing backend and link requests via a request-id header. We also emit webhooks for errors and a streaming events API for high-volume monitoring.
[03:28] Jordan Reyes: To add, the Console exposes token-by-route cost and latency; you can also ship logs to S3 or SIEM systems. For Private deployments we provide audit logs and can integrate with your KMS/HSM.
[03:42] Carlos Mendez: Security questions: SOC2 is must, encryption-at-rest, and our legal team will want KMS with HSM-backed keys for model inputs. Does Redwood support customer-managed keys in Private?
[03:56] Priya Banerjee: Yes, in Private you can bring-your-own-key via KMS integration, and for Dedicated we offer customer-managed keys for workloads on certain plans. We'll share the security pack.
[04:06] Evan Park: Network topology — if we go VPC, does Redwood connect to a peered VPC or do we run an on-prem sidecar?
[04:13] Jordan Reyes: Options: (1) Redwood Private: we deploy in your VPC with a private control plane; (2) On-prem sidecar/gateway: lightweight sidecar that proxies to Redwood's runtime (useful for air-gapped reads); (3) Dedicated with VPC peering for egress. We'll share diagrams.
[04:28] Lina Zhou: About the gateway: we currently run Kong and a small tokenization microservice. Would Redwood replace that or sit behind it?
[04:36] Priya Banerjee: Typically you keep Kong for auth and business logic and then call Redwood via the SDK or an internal gateway microservice. For lower latency you can also deploy a Redwood sidecar per cluster to reduce hop count.
[04:48] Carlos Mendez: How does failure mode look? If the primary model pool is full, do you have fallback to a cheaper model?
[04:55] Priya Banerjee: Yes, the routing policies support fallbacks — you can define a cheaper model variant and automatic fallback based on latency or capacity. We also surface rejects with structured error codes so you can automate retries.
[05:06] Evan Park: Cost controls — can we do sampling or cache prefixes?
[05:10] Priya Banerjee: We support KV/prefix caching and smart batching. Also model recommendations (quantization) per workload. We can run a profiling pass and suggest a quantized model that reduces tpu/gpu cost without big quality loss.
[05:22] Jordan Reyes: Real quick demo note: Priya will run the benchmark using your 512-token prompt and our hosted endpoints first — that'll give us the baseline for latency and cost. If that looks good we scope Dedicated with reserved capacity.
[05:34] Carlos Mendez: For the POC, what artifacts should we provide?
[05:37] Jordan Reyes: Sample traffic, authentication flow, and one or two golden prompts. Also indicate success criteria: latency p95 under 300ms, <x cost per 1k tokens, and no PII leaving the VPC if we opt for Private.
[05:49] Lina Zhou: Our legal will want the data retention policy spelled out.
[05:52] Priya Banerjee: We'll include that in the security pack, retention options for logs and payloads, and sticky sessions for KV cache TTLs.
[06:00] (crosstalk) Carlos Mendez: And, uh — SLA?
[06:03] Jordan Reyes: Hosted has best-effort; Dedicated has SLA-backed uptime and latency tiers. We'll include the SLA doc.
[06:10] Evan Park: Any gotchas with LangChain or LlamaIndex connectors? We use both in different services.
[06:16] Priya Banerjee: The connectors are maintained but tricky bits: for LlamaIndex, ensure your index stores match our chunking policy or you'll double-tokenize. For LangChain streaming and function calls, there are small differences in event ordering — our SDK docs have migration notes. Link: https://docs.redwood.ai/sdk and https://docs.redwood.ai/integrations/langchain (note: in the transcript the link may be auto-corrected).
[06:40] Jordan Reyes: Let's talk quotas and burst behavior — Priya, can you talk to the per-second token throttles?
[06:46] Priya Banerjee: Sure. On hosted, soft throttles drop below a threshold and queue slightly; rejections occur with 429 when queues overflow. For Dedicated you can set high qps and a burst bucket to handle spikes. Also we support rate limits by tag if you send user_id or api_key headers.
[07:04] Lina Zhou: Do you expose the token usage per request in a header so we can aggregate ourselves?
[07:09] Priya Banerjee: Yes — X-Redwood-Token-Used and X-Redwood-Request-Id are available for each response.
[07:16] Carlos Mendez: Observability follow-up: Can we stream token-level events into our datalake?
[07:21] Priya Banerjee: Yes, there's an events streaming endpoint and S3 hooks. High-volume customers typically use the streaming API.
[07:28] Evan Park: For the benchmark, can we replicate our concurrency pattern? We have spiky traffic with many short bursts.
[07:34] Priya Banerjee: We'll run a synthetic workload matching your rps and token histogram. Also run a cold-cache vs warm-cache pass to show KV cache benefits.
[07:44] (brief pause)
[07:52] Carlos Mendez: On the legal side, do you allow contractual clauses for data residency?
[07:57] Jordan Reyes: For Private yes; Dedicated we can agree on regions and data locality; hosted we provide region controls but some enterprise clauses require Private.
[08:06] Lina Zhou: Anything else on auth flows? We use mTLS internally for some services.
[08:11] Priya Banerjee: We support mTLS for Private and Dedicated peered endpoints; hosted uses TLS + signed tokens.
[08:18] Evan Park: Can Redwood's SDK be used inside AWS Lambda? We do some inference triggers from serverless functions.
[08:25] Priya Banerjee: Yes — both Python and Node SDKs support Lambda. Batching semantics differ; we have a sync path for short-lived functions.
[08:35] Jordan Reyes: Ok, we're at the 10 minute mark in call transcript; skipping ahead — Priya went through a quick architecture sketch (screen share) showing SDK flow, gateway pattern, and recommended KV cache locations.
[08:49] Priya Banerjee: (screen) The suggested path: Edge Gateway (auth/rate-limit) -> Internal Fetcher (tokenize + preproc) -> Redwood SDK -> Redwood runtime. For strict latency, move the preproc upstream and deploy sidecar to cut one network hop.
[09:05] Carlos Mendez: If we adopt sidecar mode, what's the ops burden?
[09:09] Priya Banerjee: Minimal. The sidecar is containerized; auto-updates are opt-in. It mainly forwards to Redwood runtime and handles local caching.
[09:18] Evan Park: Will we be charged differently if we run sidecar vs direct SDK?
[09:22] Jordan Reyes: Billing is model-usage and tokens; sidecar doesn't change the per-token billing but reduces latency and can reduce tokens via better caching.
[09:31] (noise, someone typing)
[09:41] Lina Zhou: Sample success criteria again — p95 < 300ms, warm-cache p50 < 120ms, and cost < $X per 1k tokens — we will fill in X after seeing the benchmark.
[09:53] Jordan Reyes: Sounds good. Next steps recap at end.
[10:00] (jump to 40:00 into the call, more technical deep dive)
[40:02] Priya Banerjee: Ran the synthetic run earlier with a similar customer; results showed 180ms p95 on hosted with sticky routing and warm cache; Dedicated shaved another 30-50ms at the p95. Quantized models saved ~30% cost but we had to validate quality.
[40:20] Evan Park: Important — how do you validate quality regressions? We have user-facing prompts where hallucination is critical to avoid.
[40:27] Priya Banerjee: We have an Optimize pipeline: you feed evaluation prompts and expected outputs, and we run regressions across model variants and quantization profiles; alerts if quality drops beyond a threshold.
[40:40] Carlos Mendez: For POC we want: 1) hosted benchmark; 2) evaluation set run; 3) migration plan doc for Dedicated/Private.
[40:51] Jordan Reyes: We'll deliver those. I'll own migration doc, Priya the benchmark, and we'll loop back with your infra and security.
[41:00] (wrap-up)
[41:03] Jordan Reyes: Recap: Priya runs latency/cost benchmark by Feb 12; Jordan sends security pack and pricing by Feb 6; Evan supplies traffic profile by Feb 10; schedule POC scoping for week of Feb 16–20. Any final questions?
[41:18] Carlos Mendez: None from me. Thanks for the clear options.
[41:22] Lina Zhou: Thanks — look forward to seeing the benchmark.
[41:25] Evan Park: Thanks all.
[41:28] Jordan Reyes: Great — we'll follow up with notes and links: https://docs.redwood.ai/sdk , https://docs.redwood.ai/security , and the benchmark template.
[41:40] (call ends)
